title: NewTypeIndex scans every module per import, making checks quadratic in repo size
description:
`NewTypeIndex._resolve_origin_module` resolves a dotted import name by scanning every module in the index:

    matches = [path for path in self._modules if any(path == stem or path.endswith("/" + stem) for stem in stems)]

It is called ~46 times per file checked. Cost per file is therefore proportional to the number of modules in the index, and `check_paths` builds that index from every file collected, so checking a project is O(files^2).

## This is the shipped CLI, not a corpus-tool artefact

Call path: `cli.main` -> `check_paths` (builds the index over all collected files) -> `check_file(..., project_index=index)` -> ML108/ML109 -> `_resolve_origin_module`. Nothing in scripts/ is involved.

Measured with the real `ml-lints` binary over a tree of genuine first-party source:

     files   seconds   ms/file   ratio
       489      5.82     11.90   1.00x
       978     17.71     18.10   1.52x
     1,956     60.55     30.96   2.60x
     3,912    219.28     56.05   4.71x

8x the files, 37.7x the time.

Corroborated independently at the library level against 8,000 *distinct* modules (no replication), all 21 rules, idle machine: 14.1 ms/file at 1,000 modules, 24.1 at 2,000, 41.2 at 4,000, 76.5 at 8,000 -- 5.43x for 8x, matching the CLI's 4.71x. Instrumented call counts at 4,000 modules: 6,908 resolutions over 150 files (46.1/file), each scanning all 4,000 paths = 27.6 million path comparisons for 150 files.

Note the CLI figures likely *understate* the real cost: the scaled tree has duplicate module basenames, so resolution is ambiguous and returns None early. The scan still runs, but a genuine repo of that size would resolve more names and follow more import chains.

## Impact

First-party repos in this fleet are 15-489 files; enphase_curtailer lints in ~7s, so nobody here is near the wall today. It bites any project with a few thousand first-party modules, and it is why a full all-rules corpus sweep was killed at 52 minutes unfinished against 2m51s for a single rule that makes no index lookups.

## The fix

Build the lookup as modules are ingested rather than scanning at query time. Key it on the module's final dotted component — `pkg/models.py` and `pkg/models/__init__.py` both file under "models" — so one bucket serves both stems a dotted name can match. Each resolution then tests a handful of candidates with the existing `== stem or endswith("/" + stem)` check, preserving the ambiguity semantics exactly. Bucket size is the number of modules in the project sharing a name, which does not grow with project size, so the check becomes linear in file count.

Add a test that a name matching two modules still resolves to None, and a test that asserts the candidate set a resolution consults is the same size at 10 modules as at 2,000, so a reintroduced scan fails deterministically rather than merely getting slow.

### Alternatives considered

Keying on the file basename ("common.py", "__init__.py"). Rejected: every dotted name must check both the `<name>.py` and `<name>/__init__.py` stems, so every resolution consults the `__init__.py` bucket, which holds every package in the project and grows with it (3-15% of files across this fleet). That leaves the check quadratic with a smaller constant rather than fixing it.
close_reason:
Fixed in b2e3532. Resolution now goes through a bucket keyed on the module's final dotted component, built at ingest. Measured at 150 files with the index spanning the whole tree: per-file cost was 4.30ms at 525 modules doubling to 30.07ms at 4,200; it is now flat at 0.63ms across that range, 47x faster at the top end.

The basename key the issue originally specified would not have fixed this. Both stems of a dotted name have to be checked, so every resolution consults the __init__.py bucket, and that bucket grows with the project. Keying on the final component instead files a package's __init__.py under the package's own name, collapsing both stems into one small bucket. That is recorded in the issue as an alternative considered.

title: ML701 sees only two substitution shapes, and ML700's recommended guard is defeated by memoisation
description:
Field feedback from applying 0.14 to casey_ai (~11k lines, heavy timezone/calendar code). Both rules found real defects and the messages were actionable — see "What already works" at the bottom. What follows is the gap.

Every claim here was verified against 0.14.0 in an isolated probe file, not inferred.

## ML701 sees only two syntactic shapes

The detector fires on the ternary (`ZoneInfo(x) if x else ZoneInfo("UTC")`) and the `or` form (`tz or timezone.utc`). Three equally common shapes with identical semantics are silent:

**1. Fallback via a named constant.** The indirection alone hides it — the same expression with the call inlined *is* flagged.

```python
_FALLBACK = zoneinfo.ZoneInfo("UTC")

def f(tz_name: str | None) -> zoneinfo.ZoneInfo:
    return zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(tz_name) if tz_name else _FALLBACK   # silent
```

**2. Early-return / except-arm fallback.** The most important miss, because it is how the pattern is actually written once it has any logging or error handling attached:

```python
if tz_name is None:
    _log.warning(...)
    return zoneinfo.ZoneInfo("UTC")
try:
    return zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(tz_name)
except zoneinfo.ZoneInfoNotFoundError:
    _log.warning(...)
    return zoneinfo.ZoneInfo("UTC")
```

That is `get_user_timezone` in casey_ai's `api/db/user_ops.py:342`, in a linted path, unflagged by 0.14. It is exactly what ML701's own rationale describes: "an *absent* zone counts, not only a wrong-kind one, and the fallback being a real IANA zone does not make it safe."

Worth knowing how that lands in practice: fixing the one ML701 finding 0.14 *did* report in that repo meant threading the real zone in from the caller — and the function supplying it is this unflagged instance of the same pattern. The fix terminates in the defect.

**3. Call-argument default.** `zones.get(key, timezone.utc)` is silent, while `user_tz or timezone.utc` on the following line is flagged. So it is specifically the default-argument position that is unvisited.

The other entrance found in the same sweep — a fixed offset written straight onto a datetime with `.replace(tzinfo=...)` — is [[mlp-7a8]]. It is not a fallback, so it wants its own ML7xx rather than widening this one.

## ML700's recommended fix is defeated by memoisation

`--explain ML700`'s Good Example is a runtime `isinstance` guard. That guard is silently bypassable and this cost real debugging time in casey_ai:

```python
datetime(2026, 3, 16, tzinfo=timezone.utc) == datetime(2026, 3, 16, tzinfo=ZoneInfo("UTC"))   # True
hash(...) == hash(...)                                                                        # True
```

And with the pair whose arithmetic genuinely differs:

```python
datetime(2026, 3, 16, tzinfo=ZoneInfo("Australia/Sydney")) \
    == datetime(2026, 3, 16, tzinfo=timezone(timedelta(hours=11)))   # True, and same hash
```

An `lru_cache` keyed on an aware datetime therefore cannot tell them apart. casey_ai's `expand_window_unclamped` is cached, so a warm cache skipped the new guard entirely: fixtures passed in a full suite run and failed in isolation, and running the tests was not proof the sweep was complete — the decorator had to be stripped to get a trustworthy answer.

`--explain ML700` should say so: a runtime guard on a memoised function is not load-bearing, because aware datetimes with equal offsets compare and hash equal.

## ML701 teaches "reject" where the fix is often "supply"

The message and both Good Examples point at raising. That is right only when nobody has the zone. When something upstream does, "raise" sends the author to the wrong place.

The worked case: a Google Calendar all-day node is `{"date": "2026-03-18"}` with no `timeZone`, because Google means the day in the timezone of the *calendar* the event lives on. The zone was not bad, it was out of reach — stored in Postgres, but unreachable from a `cached_property` on a Pydantic model. The fix was a method taking `calendar_tz: ZoneInfo` from the caller holding the connection, not a raise.

A second Good Example showing the parameter-threading shape alongside the raise would point authors at the right fix directly:

```python
def instant_in(self, calendar_tz: zoneinfo.ZoneInfo) -> datetime:
    """The caller holds the zone; the node never guesses one."""
    return datetime.combine(self.day, time.min, tzinfo=calendar_tz)
```

## What already works, and should not regress

- Both messages name the offending annotation and the consequence in one line. `"annotated 'object', which admits a fixed-offset tzinfo; use ZoneInfo so date arithmetic stays wall-clock"` needed no `--explain` to act on.
- ML700 reaches **attributes** and **default parameter values**, not just parameters. Both verified firing.
- The `--explain` rationale prose is the reason this got designed rather than silenced — "Wednesday 18:30 UTC is Thursday in Sydney" is what makes the stakes land.
- Accepting `str` IANA keys and unresolvable aliases/NewTypes was right: zero false positives across ~11k lines.

## Probe matrix (0.14.0)

| Shape | Verdict |
|---|---|
| `ZoneInfo(n) if n else _FALLBACK` (named constant) | silent |
| early-return / `except` arm returning `ZoneInfo("UTC")` | silent |
| `zones.get(key, timezone.utc)` | silent |
| `tz or timezone.utc` | ML701 |
| `ZoneInfo(n) if n else ZoneInfo("UTC")` inline | ML701 |
| `cached_property` returning that ternary | ML701 |
| `def f(d, tz: object)` | ML700 |
| `def f(d, tz: tzinfo = timezone.utc)` | ML700 |
| `class C: tz: tzinfo` | ML700 |

## Test cases

```python
import zoneinfo
from datetime import date, datetime, time, timedelta, timezone, tzinfo

_FALLBACK = zoneinfo.ZoneInfo("UTC")

# --- expected ML701, currently silent ---

def alias_fallback(n: str | None) -> zoneinfo.ZoneInfo:
    return zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(n) if n else _FALLBACK

def early_return_fallback(n: str | None) -> zoneinfo.ZoneInfo:
    if n is None:
        return zoneinfo.ZoneInfo("UTC")
    try:
        return zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(n)
    except zoneinfo.ZoneInfoNotFoundError:
        return zoneinfo.ZoneInfo("UTC")

def dict_default(zones: dict[str, zoneinfo.ZoneInfo], k: str) -> tzinfo:
    return zones.get(k, timezone.utc)

# --- positive controls, must keep firing ---

def or_fallback(tz: zoneinfo.ZoneInfo | None) -> tzinfo:
    return tz or timezone.utc                                    # ML701

def widened_param(d: date, tz: object) -> datetime:
    return datetime.combine(d, time(0, 0), tzinfo=tz)            # ML700

def default_param(d: date, tz: tzinfo = timezone.utc) -> datetime:
    return datetime.combine(d, time.min, tzinfo=tz)              # ML700

class Holder:
    tz: tzinfo                                                   # ML700

    def midnight(self, d: date) -> datetime:
        return datetime.combine(d, time.min, tzinfo=self.tz)
```
acceptance_criteria: The three silent shapes in the probe matrix are flagged; the positive controls still fire; --explain ML700 warns that a runtime isinstance guard on a memoised function is not load-bearing; --explain ML701 carries a second Good Example showing the zone threaded in from the caller alongside the raise.
close_reason:
Three shapes added to ML701 (named-constant fallback, guarded arm with a live sibling, lookup default), ML700 and ML701 rationales updated, ML701 retaught to name both fixes. Shipped in 8fa027f.

Verified over 36,329 files (casey_ai and enphase_curtailer, sources and both venvs): six findings, all genuine substitutions, including the get_user_timezone the report named. That sweep also caught a scope leak in the new name tracking — a zone bound locally in one function made a same-named parameter in the next look like a zone — fixed in the same commit with a regression test.

Two decisions departed from the issue as written. The memoisation warning went into BOTH rationales rather than ML700's alone: the isinstance guard it describes is ML701's good example, not ML700's, so putting it only in ML700 would have left the actual example uncaveated. And ML701's suggestion and violation message were rewritten alongside the good example, not just the example, so an author sees both fixes without reaching for --explain.

The fallthrough mirror of a presence guard (early return of the real zone, fallback as a trailing statement) is left unflagged — filed as mlp-y2k with the measurements: a working implementation bought 1 finding across the corpus while classing 168k lines as fallback arm on guards that are 99% unrelated to timezones. mlp-0kg files a CLI crash on non-UTF-8 files found during the same sweep.

title: ML702: require a literal hour=0 for the midnight-floor sink
description:
ML702 currently fires on any .replace() whose keywords include 'hour'. Measured against ../enphase_curtailer that produced 5 fires and 0 true positives, two of them because the rule cannot tell calendar flooring from scheduling.

Setting the hour to a non-zero value is never 'floor to the start of the day' -- it is 'run at 4pm'. Require the 'hour' keyword's value to be a literal 0.

Goes silent:
    app/ledger/export.py:202        hour=_EXPORT_HOUR_UTC   (= 16)
    app/training_scheduler.py:227   hour=self._config.hour_utc (default 17)
Both are deliberate UTC schedules, named as such.

Still fires, and all three remain false positives that the tightening does not reach:
    app/sun_manager.py:189          hour=0 on (now + timedelta(days=1)), where now is tz-aware but arrives as a parameter
    tests/test_dp_horizon_coverage.py:182  hour=0 on a UTC-anchored fixture
    tests/test_open_meteo_client.py:442    hour=0 on a UTC-anchored fixture

A non-literal zero -- hour=MIDNIGHT_HOUR where the constant is 0 -- goes silent too. That is the precision-first trade this rule family makes everywhere else.

Acceptance criteria:
- Only a literal 0 triggers the sink.
- Tests pin both hour=0 firing and a non-zero literal, a name, and an attribute all staying silent.
- Rule docstring and exemptions state the distinction.
- Re-measure both ../casey_ai and ../enphase_curtailer and record the counts.
close_reason:
Shipped in 961c91e. The sink now requires a literal hour=0.

Re-measured:

The two that went silent are app/ledger/export.py:202 (hour=_EXPORT_HOUR_UTC, = 16) and app/training_scheduler.py:227 (hour=self._config.hour_utc, default 17).

title: ML702: midnight floor without a zone conversion
description:
Flag .replace(hour=...) on a datetime that has not visibly been converted into a real IANA zone.

Flooring to midnight is never duration semantics -- it is unambiguously calendar intent. That is the disambiguation a timedelta unit cannot give, and it is why this rule is precise where a taint rule on +/- timedelta(days=) is not. On a fixed-offset tzinfo the floor means 'midnight at whatever offset this value happens to carry', which is 23:00 or 01:00 local across a DST transition.

The rule is a positive statement of the correct idiom, which is what api/date_utils.py:57 already does:
    start = instant.astimezone(tz).replace(hour=0, minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0)

Sink: a .replace(...) call whose keywords include hour=. Presence of hour= is the whole trigger; the other keywords are ignored.

Safe receivers (silent):
- Direct chaining: X.astimezone(...).replace(hour=...)
- One hop through a local variable assigned from .astimezone(...) earlier in the same function. This is the house idiom and appears 4 times in casey_ai already:
      local = now.astimezone(user_tz)
      floor = local.replace(hour=0, minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0)

Needs a small local-variable map -- function-scoped, no cross-function propagation, far less machinery than ML400's taint tracking. Reassignment of the local can fool it; accepted.

Silent on every other .replace keyword set:
    x.replace(tzinfo=None)      10 sites in casey_ai, including test_sync_window.py:125 and api/google_creds.py:219, both deliberate offset-stripping
    x.replace(minute=0)         hour-flooring is sub-day and offset-independent
    MONDAY.replace(year=Y + 1)  api/tests/integration/test_refuse_options_route.py:181, a far-future sentinel

Alternatives considered: extending the sink to day=/month=/year= is the same hazard one scale up, but it costs an immediate false positive on the year= sentinel above and year-bumping has nothing to do with local midnight. Revisit if a month-boundary floor ever appears.

Fixtures -- must not fire (current casey_ai):
    api/date_utils.py:57 (direct chaining)
    api/tests/integration/test_refuse_route.py:216 and api/tests/test_refuse_scope.py:63 (both direct chaining)

Known cost, accepted: three sites in casey_ai will need # noqa, and they are all tests that deliberately construct the wrong floor to assert it differs from the right one -- api/tests/test_local_day.py:117 and two calls on api/tests/test_multiplayer_phase6.py:458. Suppressing a rule on code that is deliberately the bad pattern, in order to prove the bad pattern is bad, is not the same as ignoring a finding. Say so in the rule doc.

Acceptance criteria:
- Fires on a .replace(hour=...) with an unconverted receiver, including datetime.fromisoformat(s).replace(hour=0).
- Silent on both safe-receiver shapes, direct and one-hop.
- Silent on tzinfo=, minute=-only, and day=/month=/year=.
- bad_example and good_examples per the rule contract.
- Rule doc states the deliberate-bad-pattern-in-tests noqa position.
- Tests cover each of the above plus noqa suppression.
close_reason:
Shipped in bc63d3b. Fires three times across ../casey_ai, all of them the deliberate-bad-pattern tests anticipated in the issue: api/tests/test_local_day.py:117 and two calls on api/tests/test_multiplayer_phase6.py:458. api/date_utils.py:57 and the other direct-chaining sites are silent.

One correction during implementation. A first pass treated any .astimezone(...) as a safe conversion, which let test_local_day.py:117 through -- its receiver is assigned from .astimezone(UTC), and converting to UTC produces exactly the fixed-offset value this rule exists to catch. _is_astimezone_call now rejects an argument that is a recognisable fixed offset: a UTC or timezone.utc constant, or a timezone(...) call. A bare .astimezone() still counts as a conversion, since it targets the system zone, and an argument the rule cannot resolve is assumed to be real -- ML700 polices whether that argument was typed as a ZoneInfo in the first place.

title: ML701: silent timezone substitution
description:
Flag a conditional that substitutes a timezone rather than rejecting a bad one. Encodes fail-fast-and-explicitly over swallowing the error with an invented default.

Fires on these shapes, where the substituted value is a zone construction:
    tz = x if isinstance(x, ZoneInfo) else ZoneInfo('UTC')
    tz = user_tz or UTC
    tz = tz if tz else timezone.utc

Scoped to timezones specifically -- the substituted branch must construct or name a zone.

Silent on ordinary defaulting: name = row.name or 'unknown', port = cfg.port if cfg.port else 8080.

Fixture -- must fire. casey_ai api/routes/schedule/timing.py:47, in _week_bounds (fixed in eb0229b; get the pre-fix file with git show eb0229b^:api/routes/schedule/timing.py):
    tz = today.tzinfo if isinstance(today.tzinfo, zoneinfo.ZoneInfo) else zoneinfo.ZoneInfo('UTC')

Alternatives considered: the general form (any X if isinstance(X, T) else <literal>) was rejected because 'or <default>' is far too common to include, so the general rule would have to drop to isinstance-only and would then catch less of the timezone case than this narrow rule does.

Acceptance criteria:
- Fires on all three shapes above.
- Silent on the two non-timezone defaulting shapes.
- bad_example and good_examples per the rule contract.
- Tests cover each shape, the non-timezone negatives, and noqa suppression.
close_reason:
Shipped in 160ec30. Catches the target fixture at exactly api/routes/schedule/timing.py:47 in the pre-fix tree (git show eb0229b^).

Implemented as a single unified trigger rather than three separate shape matchers: any ternary or 'or' whose fallback branch evaluates to a timezone. That covers all three specified shapes and keeps ordinary defaulting silent, because the fallback being a zone is the entire signal.

One live fire surfaced in the current casey_ai tree that the issue did not anticipate: api/google_models.py:55, where an absent Google timeZone falls back to a real ZoneInfo('UTC') rather than a fixed offset. Decided to keep it firing. The value feeds datetime.combine(d, time.min, tzinfo=tz) for an all-day event, so a wrong guess moves the event to the wrong day. Alternative considered and rejected: narrowing the rule to fire only on a fixed-offset fallback or an isinstance test, which would have gone silent here while preserving every specified must-fire. Rejected because 'absent zone' is a guess too, and a real IANA fallback does not make the guess correct. The rationale now says so explicitly.

title: ML700: timezone parameter must be a real zone
description:
Flag parameters and class attributes that carry a timezone but are not typed as a real IANA zone. A widened annotation is where a fixed-offset tzinfo enters the system, and it is the cheapest place to stop it -- purely local, no dataflow.

Adds RuleCategory.TIME_CORRECTNESS (first ML7xx rule).

Fires on:
- A parameter or class attribute (dataclass field or Pydantic model field) whose name is tz, tzinfo, timezone or zone, or ends with _tz, _timezone or _zone, annotated object, Any, tzinfo or datetime.tzinfo, or left unannotated.
- Any parameter annotated bare tzinfo or datetime.tzinfo, whatever its name. That annotation is almost always a widening mistake and the trigger is name-independent.

Silent on:
- str. A string cannot do datetime arithmetic so it cannot cause the defect, and boundary code legitimately carries IANA keys as strings.
- ZoneInfo, zoneinfo.ZoneInfo, and any union containing one, including ZoneInfo | None.
- Any annotation the AST cannot resolve, such as a local alias or NewType. Silence is the honest answer when the name is opaque.
- self, cls, *args, **kwargs and lambda parameters.

Return annotations are out of scope. Return names cannot be matched, so the trigger would have to be annotation-driven alone, and '-> object' has legitimate uses unrelated to timezones -- it would become a general no-Any-returns rule wearing a timezone hat.

Fixture -- must fire. casey_ai api/solver/window.py:132:
    def _hm_to_datetime(d: date, hm: _TimeHM, tz: object) -> datetime:
with the sink at line 137, datetime.combine(d, time(0, 0), tzinfo=tz) behind a type: ignore[arg-type]. This rule catches it at the point the type: ignore was written.

This also covers the 'calendar anchor built from a date plus an arbitrary tzinfo' shape -- datetime.combine(d, time(0,0), tzinfo=tz) then + timedelta(hours=...) -- which no timedelta-unit heuristic can reach, because the unit is hours.

Fixtures -- must not fire. All are current casey_ai code:
    timezone: str                       (api/calendar_sync.py:190, api/schemas/calendar.py:37)
    user_tz: ZoneInfo | None = None     (api/calendar_service.py:178, api/maps_client.py:239, :411)
    user_tz: _BatchUserTz               (api/calendar_sync.py:587)
    tz: zoneinfo.ZoneInfo               (api/date_utils.py:30, :61, :75 and many more)

Known limitation, accepted: an alias such as _BatchUserTz = object defeats the rule. The AST cannot resolve it, and firing on every unresolvable alias would punish exactly the wrap-it-in-a-real-type habit the project asks for.

Acceptance criteria:
- Rule fires exactly once against the pre-fix api/solver/window.py.
- Rule is silent on every must-not-fire fixture above.
- bad_example and good_examples per the rule contract.
- Tests cover: positive, each must-not-fire shape, unannotated parameter, bare tzinfo under a non-matching name, noqa suppression.

title: E: Timezone correctness rules (ML700-ML702)
description:
Wall-clock date arithmetic performed on a datetime whose tzinfo is not a real IANA zone.

Adding timedelta(days=)/timedelta(weeks=) to an aware datetime is wall-clock arithmetic -- landing on the same local time on a later day -- only when the tzinfo is a ZoneInfo. With a fixed-offset tzinfo (timezone.utc, timezone(timedelta(hours=10)), or what psycopg hands back for a timestamptz) the identical expression becomes absolute arithmetic: exactly 24h or 168h, landing an hour off local midnight across a DST transition. The same applies to .replace(hour=0, ...), which then means 'midnight at whatever offset this value happens to carry' rather than local midnight.

Three real defects in ../casey_ai motivated this. An AST linter cannot see a tzinfo's runtime type, and the most dangerous source -- a timestamptz out of psycopg -- is statically invisible. These rules are a net, not a proof: they catch the statically visible sources and leave the rest to runtime guards.

Precision beats recall on every design call. ml-lints consumers are forbidden from ignoring lint rules, so a rule that fires on correct code is far more expensive than one that misses cases.

Rationale text for all three rules is lifted from the local_day docstring in casey_ai api/date_utils.py, which is the best existing statement of the hazard.

Alternatives considered:

A taint rule (ML400-shaped) flagging tainted +/- timedelta(days=|weeks=) was rejected on measured precision. Across casey_ai there are 24 non-test timedelta(days=) sites, 12 of them literally datetime.now(UTC) +/- timedelta(days=N) -- log cutoffs, cache TTLs, watch lifetimes, lookback periods. All correct, all would fire: 12 false positives against 1 true positive. Restricting to weeks= only leaves 3 false positives against 1 true positive. days= is genuinely ambiguous between 'N days of elapsed time' and 'same clock time N days later', and intent is not in the AST. ML702's hour= sink is the precise substitute: flooring to midnight is never duration semantics.

An architectural rule (day-or-larger arithmetic must live in one blessed module) was deferred. It needs a 24-entry allowlist at day scale, and 'outside api/date_utils.py' is a consumer-specific fact -- cli.py parses only select/ignore/exclude today, so it would require new per-rule config plumbing.
close_reason:
All three rules shipped: ML700 in b8e2437, ML701 in 160ec30, ML702 in bc63d3b. Adds RuleCategory.TIME_CORRECTNESS.

Measured against ../casey_ai, the three fire five times in total and every fire is intended:
- ML700 once, api/solver/window.py:132 -- the tz: object behind a type: ignore[arg-type].
- ML701 once, api/google_models.py:55 -- an absent Google timeZone defaulting to ZoneInfo('UTC'), kept as a true positive because the value floors an all-day event and a wrong guess moves it to the wrong day.
- ML702 three times, all in tests that deliberately construct the wrong floor to assert it is wrong: api/tests/test_local_day.py:117 and two calls on api/tests/test_multiplayer_phase6.py:458.

ML701 also catches the historical defect at api/routes/schedule/timing.py:47 in the pre-fix tree (eb0229b^), verified directly.

Two of the three original defects are now caught at the point of authorship. The third (casey-47x0, datetime.fromisoformat + timedelta(weeks=1) spanning two functions in a test) is deliberately not caught -- see the taint-rule rejection in this epic's description.

Leftovers filed: ML703, the deferred architectural rule, blocked on per-rule config in cli.py; and a note that all three need TypeScript counterparts when the port's conformance gates land.

title: F5: Structured reporting and message ids in Python
description: messageIds becomes a required manifest field (T1) and the behavioural conformance corpus (T12) asserts a messageId plus data payload per finding, so Python must report structurally instead of pre-formatting a sentence at the call site. report() gains a message-id-plus-data form and each rule declares the ids it can emit. Wide but shallow: 20 self.report call sites plus ML400's direct Violation construction, and 17 of 19 rules emit exactly one message. Violation.format's output stays byte-identical - the rendered sentence is still what users see, now produced from the id and the data rather than passed in.
acceptance_criteria: Every rule declares a non-empty messageIds, asserted by a test rather than left to review. Rendered output byte-unchanged for every rule's bad_example, asserted by test. Lands before T3, which serialises the field.

title: F4: Rename Rule.code to Rule.id across the Python package
description:
See docs/typescript-port.md#F4. D1 named the manifest field 'id' (ESLint's word for @ml-lints/ML500 is the rule ID, and 'code' collides with badExample/goodExamples, which hold literal source code). Rather than leave a permanent seam where the manifest says 'id' and Python says 'code', rename the Python side to match.

Scope: RuleCode StrEnum -> RuleId (violation.py); Violation.code -> Violation.id; Rule.code ClassVar (rules/__init__.py:69) and its 19 rule-module assignments; cls.code readers in runner.py:35, cli.py:312-519, rules/__init__.py:91-95; has_noqa's 'code' parameter (noqa.py:12); both rule templates (src/ml_lints/rules/_template.py, tests/rules/_template.py); scripts/generate_rule_docs.py and generate_rules_table.py; tests/. Prose in README.md and CONTRIBUTING_RULES.md (:24 'Rule code ranges', :51, :168-177).

NOT in scope, because these carry the value rather than the field name and renaming them would be a user-visible break: the '# noqa: ML100' suppression syntax, and Violation.format()'s 'path:line:col: ML100 message' output.

Land this BEFORE T3 (mlp-v00.4) so the manifest emitter reads rule.id directly with no mapping line, and so T1's seam paragraph is deleted rather than implemented.

Collision risk: justfile:101's inline 'python3 -c' scaffolding hardcodes the '# -- add new codes above this line --' sentinel in violation.py and prints 'RuleCode.${code}'. It must move in lockstep. A1 (language-aware scaffolding) plans to extract that same one-liner into scripts/scaffold_rule.py — whichever lands second rebases onto the first.

Note: ruff's A003 does not fire on 'id' as a class attribute under this project's select=["ALL"] config — verified empirically, so the rename is not blocked by linting.
acceptance_criteria: No 'code' identifier remains as a rule-identifier field name in src/, scripts/ or tests/ (grep-verified); RuleCode is RuleId. 'just new-rule ML999' still scaffolds a working rule and injects the enum member. 'just precommit' green. The suppression syntax '# noqa: ML100' and the 'path:line:col: ML100 message' output format are byte-unchanged — asserted by an existing or added test. docs/typescript-port.md's T1 seam paragraph deleted, since the seam no longer exists.

title: T12: Behavioural conformance corpus for naive ML500
description:
Instantiates the two-tier behavioural conformance mechanism specified by D2 in docs/typescript-port.md, for the tracer's one shared rule.

Tier 1 (scenario catalogue): a scenario set covering span classification - identifier, comment, doc comment, plain string literal - with both polarities, realised independently in each language at packages/<lang>/conformance/ML500.json.

Tier 2 (answer key): shared/conformance/answers/ML500.json, covering word-splitting (camelCase, snake_case, kebab-case, digit runs), case restoration, whole-name reconstruction, URL and dotted-name skipping, and offsets across newlines.

Plus the two runners and the two adapters. Both tiers drive the real linter end to end, never a rule-internal helper. Scoped to naive ML500: no exemptions, because those are K1 and divergent by design.
acceptance_criteria: Must demonstrably FAIL when one implementation's word-splitting is changed and the other's is not; when case restoration is dropped in one language; when one language stops scanning doc comments; when a claimed scenario loses its realisation; and when an adapter returns a constant offset. Must PASS when one language's rendered message sentence is reworded. Failure messages quote the input, both expected sides and both actual sides verbatim. Wired into just ci as its OWN recipe, separate from T8's - this one needs both toolchains and T8's needs neither, so a Python-only contributor is told which half they cannot run.

title: Audit all 1,761 ML500 spelling-map entries for homographs, sense changes and archaic forms
description:
ML500's spelling map holds 1,761 American→Australian entries. Nothing checks them, and they are wrong often enough to matter: `ax` → `axe` was removed in 94eee54 after it flagged every matplotlib axes variable, and mlp-q93 lists nine more found by reading the top of a corpus frequency table. Those nine were found because they were common. The tail has never been looked at.

Audit all 1,761 entries for the three classes that have produced every error found so far.

## The three classes

**Homograph** — the key is also standard Australian English in another sense, so the rule is right only for one meaning. `tire` → `tyre` is correct for the noun and wrong for the verb. `ax` → `axe` was this: correct for the tool, wrong for every matplotlib axes.

**Different word** — the key and value are not spellings of the same word at all. `ton` → `tonne` converts between units that differ by 10% (2,240 lb against 1,000 kg). `bevy` → `bevvy` turns a group into a drink.

**Archaic value** — the suggestion is a real British form but not current Australian usage. `reflection` → `reflexion`, and its `-xion` siblings.

## Method

Work the whole map, not the corpus frequency table — the point of this task is the entries too rare to show up in a sweep. For each entry ask whether the key is ever correct Australian English, and whether the value is what Macquarie actually gives.

Measure the effect with `just corpus-lint ML500`, which takes about three minutes over the ~60,000-file corpus; `just corpus-diff ML500` reports only what a change added or removed. CONTRIBUTING_RULES.md has the workflow, and .corpus.toml.example the setup. Findings in site-packages count: third-party code is not ours to rewrite, but a hit there is still the rule being right or wrong, which is the only question this task asks.

## Two entries already known to need a decision

`gray` → `grey` (611 corpus hits): correct for the colour, but `gray` is also the SI unit of absorbed dose (Gy) and a matplotlib colormap name.

`analog` → `analogue` (737): defensible as prose, near-universal in electronics identifiers including this fleet's own Home Assistant work.

## Acceptance

Every entry has been looked at. Entries in the three classes are removed or narrowed, with the reasoning recorded for any that were considered and kept — otherwise the next reader re-derives the same judgements. A before/after `just corpus-lint ML500` quantifies the change.

title: ML500's spelling map has entries that are wrong in any codebase
description:
The first all-rules corpus sweep surfaced `ax` → `axe`, removed in 94eee54. Reading the rest of ML500's 156,562 findings by flagged word turns up more entries that are wrong in any codebase, not merely unactionable in someone else's. Together they account for 4,624 findings.

| entry | suggests | corpus hits | why it is wrong |
|---|---|---:|---|
| `licensed` | licenced | 3,831 | Australian English splits the noun from the verb: `licence` is the noun, `license` the verb. The verb's inflections keep the -s-, so `licensed` is already correct. `defense`/`offense`/`pretense` in the same map are right, because those are noun-only. |
| `reflection` | reflexion | 623 | `-xion` is an archaic British form. Macquarie gives `reflection`. |
| `deflection` | deflexion | 87 | As above. |
| `licensing` | licencing | 53 | Verb form, as `licensed`. |
| `ton` | tonne | 22 | Not a spelling variant — a ton and a tonne are different units (2,240 lb against 1,000 kg). Converting one to the other changes the meaning. |
| `tons` | tonnes | 5 | As above. |
| `inflection` | inflexion | 2 | As above for `-xion`. |
| `tire` | tyre | 1 | Homograph: the verb ("to tire") is correct Australian English. Only the noun is `tyre`. |
| `bevy` | bevvy | 0 | Different words: a `bevy` is a group, a `bevvy` is a drink. No corpus hits, but wrong whenever it fires. |

## Two the sweep raises without settling

`gray` → `grey` (611 hits). Correct for the colour, but `gray` is also the SI unit of absorbed dose (Gy) and a matplotlib colormap name.

`analog` → `analogue` (737 hits). Defensible as prose, but `analog` is near-universal in electronics identifiers, including the ones in this fleet's own Home Assistant work.

## Scope

These nine entries, and nothing else. They are wrong on their face and each is a one-line deletion. The map's other 1,752 entries have never been audited and almost certainly hold more of the same three defect classes — homographs, pairs that differ in sense, archaic values — but finding them means reading the whole map rather than the top of a frequency table. That is mlp-c47.
close_reason:
Fixed in a07d2b5. All nine entries removed, along with four inflected siblings the table did not list (analogs, bevies, inflections, tires) and analog itself, which the issue had parked as undecided.

Measured over the 60,537-file corpus: ML500 goes from 156,562 hits across 23,060 files to 150,632 across 20,928. The drop in files hit (9.2%) is proportionally larger than the drop in hits (3.8%), because licensed fired once or twice in each of thousands of licence headers rather than many times in a few files.

gray is deliberately kept. It is correct for the colour, and the SI-unit and matplotlib-colormap senses are a narrowing decision rather than a deletion. It carries over to mlp-c47 with the rest of the unaudited map.

title: ML500 is 80% of the all-rules corpus sweep, burying every other rule
description:
On the all-rules corpus sweep (60,537 files, 11 roots) ML500 is 156,562 of 196,065 findings — 80% of the report, at 2,586 per 1,000 files against 214 for the next rule. Every other rule's findings are buried, which blunts the sweep that `just corpus-lint` exists to provide.

The cause is what is being swept, not the rule.

## Virtualenvs, not the wordlist

| corpus | files | ML500 hits | per 1K | share of all findings |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| including venvs | 60,537 | 156,562 | 2,586 | 80% |
| first-party only | 3,568 | 1,178 | 330 | 58% |

Site-packages carries roughly eight times the rate of first-party source. That is not the rule misfiring — `initialized`, `normalization` and `colors` in third-party code are correctly identified American spellings. They are simply findings about code that is not ours to rewrite, and there are 155,000 of them.

Sweeping venvs is deliberate and should stay: site-packages is the harshest false-positive detector the corpus has, and it is how ML103, ML300 and others earn their evidence. The problem is that one rule's correct-but-unactionable output swamps the report the sweep prints.

## First-party hits are mostly genuine

The 1,178 first-party hits are led by `color`/`colour` (95), `behavior`/`behaviour` (88), `normalized` (54), `Initialize` (33) and `optimization` (33) — real American spellings in our own code, which is what the rule is for.

One sub-case is not: identifiers fixed by a third-party API, such as `ColorMode` and `ColorOrder` (Home Assistant) and `AnalogInputType`. Renaming those breaks the integration. Whether ML500 should recognise a name it cannot own is a separate question from the volume problem, and smaller.

## What to decide

Where the fix belongs: capping or collapsing one rule's contribution to the sampled report, excluding venvs for high-volume spelling-class rules specifically, or reporting first-party and venv rates as separate columns so a rule's real signal is visible next to its noise. Measure with `just corpus-lint ML500` before and after.

## Alternatives considered

Trimming the wordlist. `ax` was removed in 94eee54 after the first sweep flagged every matplotlib axes variable as `axe`. It cut 32,292 hits — a 17% reduction that moved ML500's share from 83% to 80%. The wordlist is worth fixing when an entry is wrong, but it is not the lever for this problem: the remaining 156,562 hits are overwhelmingly correct.

title: No way to measure a rule's false negatives
description:
`just corpus-lint` (mlp-jim) measures false positives: it prints what a rule fires on, and you read the samples and judge them. There is no equivalent for the opposite error -- code that should have tripped a rule and did not.

## Why this needs its own technique

A false positive announces itself. A false negative is silent by construction: it is a line somewhere in the corpus that should have been flagged and was not, and nothing in the sweep output points anywhere near it. No amount of reading `corpus-lint` output can find one. Every workable approach is a way of manufacturing a cheap *second, independent opinion* about what should have fired.

## Scope the corpus differently

Sweep first-party source only (`include-venvs = false`), not the full 60k-file corpus. The venv-heavy corpus is excellent for false positives and poor for false negatives: a missed violation in `pendulum` is not something anyone would fix, and third-party code follows conventions the rules were never written for, so the "misses" are mostly not misses. First-party source is ~10k files and every finding is actionable.

## Build: negative-space sampling

Add a `--negative-space` mode to scripts/corpus_lint.py. Grep the corpus for the rule's subject matter, subtract the files where the rule fired, and print a random sample of the remainder to read.

Worked example: 334 corpus files mention `ZoneInfo`/`tzinfo`/`timezone.utc`; ML701 fires in 4. The other 330 are the negative space. Sample 30, read them, count genuine misses -- a recall estimate with arithmetic behind it.

Needs a per-rule subject-matter pattern. Natural home is a class attribute on the rule alongside `bad_example`/`good_examples`, which also makes it reviewable when the rule is written. A rule without one is skipped by this mode and says so.

## Alternatives considered

Recorded so they are not re-proposed:

- **Cross-tool differential.** Run another linter with an overlapping rule over the same corpus and look at what it flags that we do not. Ruff's DTZ family overlaps ML700/ML701. Nearly free, genuinely independent, no rule-writing -- but only covers rules with an external analogue. ML500, ML600 and ML201 get nothing. Worth doing opportunistically, not worth building infrastructure for.
- **Over-broad recall net.** Per rule, a crude high-recall/low-precision twin; the net-minus-rule gap is exactly the set of excluded cases, which you read to sort deliberate from accidental. Highest signal of any option, but it is a second rule to write and maintain per real rule. Reach for it on a specific rule you distrust, not as policy.
- **Sample-and-read with no net.** Random N files read against the rule's definition. The only unbiased recall number, and the only method that can surface a shape nobody conceived of. Cost is entirely reading. Keep as a periodic audit.
- **Seeding synthetic violations into the corpus. Rejected.** It only measures recall on shapes already thought of -- the same population the unit tests cover -- so it re-runs the test suite in a noisier room.

title: just precommit never runs ml-lints over this repo's own source
description:
This project lints itself with ruff and ty, but never with its own rules. `just lint` runs `ruff format`, `ruff check` and `ty check`; nothing anywhere in the justfile, .githooks/pre-commit or .github/workflows/ci.yml invokes `ml-lints`. The tool has 22 rules encoding this repo's own style policy, and that policy is unenforced on the repo that defines it.

## What to add

An `extra-lints` recipe that runs the working-tree version of ml-lints over `src/`, `scripts/` and `tests/`, wired into `just precommit` and into CI as its own step, per the Checks Architecture section: the recipe is the source of truth, CI and the hook only call it.

## The thing to decide

`tests/` deliberately contains code that violates the rules -- fixtures are the point of the test suite. Either exclude `tests/` from the sweep, or keep it in and settle how fixtures suppress: `# noqa` (the noqa module already exists) versus a path exclusion in pyproject.toml's `[tool.ml-lints]` table. Choosing per-fixture noqa keeps the coverage; a blanket exclusion is cheaper but leaves test helper code unchecked.

Expect the first run to surface real violations in src/ and scripts/. Fixing those is part of this task, not a follow-up -- a recipe that is added already failing is not wired in.

## Not the corpus sweep

Distinct from mlp-jim, which sweeps *external* checkouts for false positives and is deliberately not a gate. This one is a gate, and only covers this repo.

title: ML701 treats a zone derived from a value as an invented one
description:
ML701 learned to see a fallback hidden behind a name (`_FALLBACK = ZoneInfo("UTC")`) in
8fa027f. The binding test is `_is_zone_literal`, which accepts any `ZoneInfo(...)` call
regardless of its argument -- so a name assigned a zone *derived from a value* is
treated the same as one assigned an *invented* zone. Falling back to the derived name
then reads as a substitution when it is not.

The shape, reduced from `astral/sun.py` (4 occurrences, lines 711, 783, 854, 928):

```python
def dawn(tzinfo, date):
    if isinstance(tzinfo, str):
        tzinfo = zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(tzinfo)   # binds the name -> now "a zone"
    ...
    tzinfo = date.tzinfo or tzinfo           # ML701 fires here
```

The fallback is the zone the *caller supplied*. That is the fix ML701's own message
recommends ("take the zone from the caller that has it"), so the rule is flagging the
good outcome. Nothing was invented.

## Where it is

`src/ml_lints/rules/ml701_timezone_substitution.py`, `ML701._note_zone_binding` ->
`_is_zone_literal`.

## The distinction that fixes it

`_FALLBACK = ZoneInfo("UTC")` invents a zone; `tzinfo = ZoneInfo(tzinfo)` derives one.
Only bind a name when the zone is built from a constant -- a literal argument, or a
`UTC` / `timezone.utc` constant.

Prototyped (two lines in `_note_zone_binding`, rejecting a Call whose first argument is
not an `ast.Constant`) and measured:

| Case | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `astral/sun.py` (the FP above) | 4 | **0** |
| `psycopg/_tz.py` `return zi` | 1 | 1 |
| `_FALLBACK` case from mlp-wgo | 1 | 1 |
| Full test suite | 355 pass | 355 pass |

`psycopg` survives because `zi` is bound twice -- to `ZoneInfo(sname)` (derived) *and*
to `timezone.utc` (constant); the constant binding is the one that matters.

## Decide as part of the fix

A constant-only test would also drop `_FALLBACK = ZoneInfo(_DEFAULT_ZONE_NAME)`, where
the argument is a module-level string constant. That is still an invented zone and
arguably should stay flagged, which would mean resolving constant *strings* too rather
than requiring a literal at the call.
acceptance_criteria: A name bound to a zone built from a variable is not treated as an invented fallback; the astral/sun.py shape is silent while the _FALLBACK case from mlp-wgo and psycopg's 'return zi' both still fire.
close_reason:
Fixed in 0025a75. A zone counts as invented only when its identity was fixed at authoring time, so the astral/sun.py shape (tzinfo rebound to ZoneInfo(tzinfo), then date.tzinfo or tzinfo) is silent.

Three decisions were settled during the fix, the first being the one the issue deferred:

- Module-level string constants ARE resolved, so ZoneInfo(_DEFAULT_ZONE_NAME) stays flagged. The corpus evidence favoured a literal-only test (the shape occurs once in 18,589 files and is never a fallback), but that test would call two spellings of the same program different things. Correctness over the cheaper proxy, at Mike's direction.
- The exemption covers ZoneInfo alone. timezone(...) yields a fixed offset however the offset was arrived at, and a fixed offset is never the zone the caller had, so timezone(timedelta(hours=11)) is still invented. Matches the existing _IANA_CONSTRUCTORS split.
- Inline and through-a-name are treated alike. x or ZoneInfo(user.tz_name) is now silent too, rather than leaving the rule with two views of one expression. This widened the change past the issue's stated _note_zone_binding scope.

Only module-level string constants are resolved; an imported name or a local string leaves the zone looking derived. Recorded in the exemptions text rather than left as a silent limit.

Measured: 7 corpus findings before, 3 after. Four astral false positives gone, psycopg's 'return zi' and both casey_ai/db/user_ops.py findings kept. 360 tests pass (5 new).

title: ml-lints crashes on a file that is not valid UTF-8
description:
`ml-lints` aborts with a traceback the moment it meets a file it cannot decode as UTF-8.
One such file anywhere in the tree kills the whole run, so nothing is reported for the
thousands of files that were fine.

```
File "src/ml_lints/runner.py", line 30, in check_file
    source = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xa4 in position 64: invalid start byte
```

Reproduced while sweeping a venv's site-packages; it made the CLI unusable for that
corpus and the sweep had to be run through a hand-written driver instead.

The inconsistency is internal: `check_paths`' index pre-pass already guards this exact
case, skipping files that raise `OSError`, `SyntaxError` or `UnicodeDecodeError`
(`runner.py:63-66`). The per-file pass that follows has no such guard, so a file the
pre-pass deliberately tolerated then crashes the run.

Worth deciding as part of the fix: a file that cannot be read is arguably worth one
diagnostic line rather than silence, since a linter that quietly skips input can report
a clean run over files it never opened.
acceptance_criteria: A non-UTF-8 (or otherwise unreadable) file does not abort the run; the remaining files are still checked, and the skip is visible to the user rather than silent.

title: ML701 misses the fallthrough mirror of a presence guard
description:
ML701 treats a guarded arm as the `if` body (absence test) or the explicit `else` block
(presence test). The fallthrough mirror -- an early return of the real zone, with the
fallback as a plain trailing statement -- is silent:

```python
# covered: absence guard
if tz_name is None:
    return ZoneInfo("UTC")      # flagged
return ZoneInfo(tz_name)

# covered: presence test, explicit else
if tz_name is not None:
    return ZoneInfo(tz_name)
else:
    return ZoneInfo("UTC")      # flagged

# THE GAP: presence test, fallthrough
if tz_name is not None:
    return ZoneInfo(tz_name)
return ZoneInfo("UTC")          # silent
```

All three are the same defect, and ruff's RET505 pushes authors towards the third.

## Why it was left out

Closing the gap means treating "the statements after a terminating presence guard" as
the fallback arm. That inference is sound, but it replaces a precise anchor with a
positional one: the covered shapes anchor the fallback to a test whose body or `else`
*is* the fallback, so the guard is necessarily about the zone being substituted. The
fallthrough form has no such anchor -- any terminating guard opens the region.

A working implementation was built and measured over 36,329 files (casey_ai and
enphase_curtailer, sources and both venvs):

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| New findings over the shipped rule | **1** |
| Widened regions opened | 12,437 |
| Lines newly classed as fallback arm | 168,491 |
| Opened by a bare `if x:` guard | 70% |
| Guard mentions tz/zone/utc/time | **1%** |
| Median / 95th pct / longest region | 4 / 53 / 888 lines |

The single new finding was `tzlocal/unix.py:221`. That function does substitute UTC, so
the verdict is right -- but it fired because of `if tzenv: return tzenv` 29 lines
earlier, reported the function's single exit rather than the substitution, and rendered
the fallback as `'tz'`. Right answer, wrong reason, wrong line.

Neither first-party codebase gained a finding.

## Alternatives considered

Open the region only when the guard tests a zone-named variable, reusing ML700's
`_ZONE_NAMES` / `_ZONE_SUFFIXES`. This restores the anchor and cuts the new surface by
~99% (it would not have fired on tzlocal, whose guard is `tzenv`). Worth reaching for
first if this gap is ever reported from the field -- it is the cheap version.
acceptance_criteria: The fallthrough form is flagged without materially widening what counts as a guarded position; the tzlocal/unix.py shape either stays silent or reports the substitution rather than the function's exit.

title: A fixed offset written directly via .replace(tzinfo=...) is invisible to both ML700 and ML701
description:
`.replace(tzinfo=...)` with a fixed offset is invisible to both ML700 and ML701. Verified silent against 0.14.0:

```python
d.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)
d.replace(tzinfo=timezone(timedelta(hours=11)))
```

## Why this is not an ML701 gap

ML701 is about a *fallback*: a zone that is absent or of the wrong kind, and a substituted guess standing in for it. The `else` branch is the defect, and the fix is to reject rather than invent.

`.replace(tzinfo=...)` has no fallback in it. Nothing is missing, nothing is being stood in for — it is a direct, unconditional write of a fixed offset onto a datetime. There is no bad value arriving from a caller to reject, so ML701's suggestion ("raise instead so the caller that supplied it gets fixed") does not describe the fix, and folding it into ML701 would make that rule's message wrong for half the cases it reports.

It is also not ML700, which governs *annotations* — the places a fixed offset can enter through a widened type. This is the other entrance: code that manufactures one itself.

So it wants its own rule in the ML7xx range, with its own suggestion: re-express the instant with `astimezone(ZoneInfo(...))`, or attach a real IANA zone, rather than stamping an offset.

## Why it is worth having

This is the most direct injection of the defect the ML7xx family exists to prevent. ML700 stops a fixed offset entering through a signature; this stops code creating one from nothing and attaching it to a value that then flows on. Everything downstream — `+ timedelta(days=1)`, `.replace(hour=0)`, week bucketing — silently degrades from wall-clock to absolute, which is the whole premise of ML700's rationale.

The `timezone.utc` case matters as much as the offset case despite UTC having no DST: the resulting value is still a fixed-offset `tzinfo`, so it fails ML700's `isinstance` guards downstream and poisons arithmetic once it is converted into a local zone.

## Note on detection

Both rules' tests should keep a case asserting `.replace(tzinfo=ZoneInfo("Australia/Sydney"))` is *not* flagged — attaching a real IANA zone via `replace` is legitimate (it is how a naive datetime gets localised) and must stay silent.

## Test cases

```python
import zoneinfo
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

# --- expected to flag ---

def stamped_utc(d: datetime) -> datetime:
    return d.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)

def stamped_fixed_offset(d: datetime) -> datetime:
    return d.replace(tzinfo=timezone(timedelta(hours=11)))

# --- must stay silent: attaching a real IANA zone ---

def localised(d: datetime) -> datetime:
    return d.replace(tzinfo=zoneinfo.ZoneInfo("Australia/Sydney"))
```
acceptance_criteria: A new ML7xx rule flags .replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc) and .replace(tzinfo=timezone(timedelta(...))), with a suggestion naming astimezone/ZoneInfo rather than raising; .replace(tzinfo=ZoneInfo(...)) with a real IANA zone stays silent; ML700 and ML701 are unchanged.

title: Decide ML702's fate: 6 fires, 0 true positives across two repos
description:
ML702 has now been measured against two large codebases and has not yet caught a real defect.

  ../casey_ai            3 fires, all deliberate-bad-pattern tests that construct the wrong floor in order to assert it is wrong (test_local_day.py:117, test_multiplayer_phase6.py:458 x2)
  ../enphase_curtailer   3 fires, all correct code:
      app/sun_manager.py:189            hour=0 on (now + timedelta(days=1)); now is tz-aware but arrives as a parameter, so the rule cannot see the conversion
      tests/test_dp_horizon_coverage.py:182  hour=0 on a UTC-anchored fixture doing deliberate absolute arithmetic
      tests/test_open_meteo_client.py:442    same; its docstring says 'checked as absolute times rather than day counts'

The literal-hour=0 tightening (mlp-1ps) removed the scheduling false positives and is worth keeping regardless. It did not change the underlying picture.

The rule was accepted on an explicit 'a net for the future, not a catch for the past' premise, with an estimated cost of 2 suppressions. The measured cost is 6, and consumers are forbidden from ignoring lint rules.

Two of the three remaining enphase fires share one shape worth investigating before deciding: flooring a value that is visibly constructed with tzinfo=UTC. Whether that is distinguishable from the casey_ai true-positive shape (flooring a value assigned from .astimezone(UTC)) decides whether the rule can be rescued -- they may be the same thing, in which case it cannot.

The sun_manager fire is a different and more tractable gap: the receiver is a BinOp over a tz-aware parameter. Seeing through BinOp to its left operand would not fix it (the operand is still an unresolvable parameter), but treating datetime.now(tz=X) as a conversion where X is not a fixed offset would help elsewhere.

Decide: rescue, downgrade to opt-in, or revert bc63d3b and 961c91e.

ML702 is now reverted from main in 2be10e4, which undoes bc63d3b (the rule) and 961c91e (the literal-hour=0 tightening). It is off for consumers while this decision is open rather than shipping as a default-on rule with a 0-for-6 record.

Nothing is lost. Both SHAs are recorded above and in the revert message, so a rescue is a cherry-pick of the two commits plus whatever this issue decides to change. RuleCode.ML702 is freed and should be reused rather than skipped if the rule comes back.

Note for whoever picks this up: the revert conflicted on .beads/issues.jsonl both times, because reverting those commits would also roll back beads state that has since moved on. title: Corpus sweep runs on one core of ten
description:
`just corpus-lint` sweeps ~60,500 files serially. Nothing in ml_lints is parallel -- no multiprocessing, no concurrent.futures, no --jobs flag -- and `check_paths` is a plain `for path in paths` loop. Observed at 100% CPU on a 10-core machine: one core busy, nine idle. A full all-rules sweep takes ~30 minutes.

## What to do

Add a process pool to scripts/corpus_lint.py, over files *within* each root, after that root's NewTypeIndex is built. Per-file checking is independent and the findings are already plain data (`Finding` is a NamedTuple built for exactly this kind of crossing), so the fan-out is straightforward.

The index is the awkward part: it is per-root and must be shared by every worker checking that root. Either build it in the parent and let fork share it (fine on Linux/macOS, wrong on spawn), or build it once per worker and accept the duplication. Measure before choosing -- index construction is a second parse of the whole root, so rebuilding it per worker may cost more than it saves.

Workers default to os.cpu_count(); a `--jobs` flag is worth having so a diagnosis run can force serial execution.

## Deliberately scoped to the sweep

This is a change to the corpus script, not to `ml_lints.runner` or the CLI. Parallelising the library is a separate question with different trade-offs -- normal CLI runs are over small file sets where process startup would dominate.

## Do not do this first

mlp-kzi, the rule-set scaling investigation, should land first or at least be understood first. A 10x from cores would mask whatever is making the full rule set scale badly, and that is the finding that affects real users rather than just this tool.

title: Corpus sweep: the all-rules run is unmeasured and the docs still warn it is impractical
description:
Measuring a rule's false-positive rate against the sibling-repo corpus is the standard evidence step before shipping or changing a rule — it decided mlp-wgo's widen-or-not question and mlp-91c's three design choices, and it independently caught a scope-leak bug in a rule under development. It was entirely manual, with every rule change re-deriving the same throwaway script, which GEMINI.md prohibits: 'NEVER rely on manual steps ... If a step is required, add it to the justfile.'

## What exists

`just corpus-lint [CODE...]` and `just corpus-diff [CODE...]`, backed by `scripts/corpus_lint.py`, with the corpus location in a gitignored `.corpus.toml` (validated with Pydantic, `.corpus.toml.example` committed) and a walkthrough in CONTRIBUTING_RULES.md. Neither recipe is a gate: both depend on checkouts outside this repo, so precommit and CI do not call them.

The recipes drive `runner.check_file` directly rather than the CLI, which excludes `.venv` by default — where most of the corpus lives — and aborts on the first non-UTF-8 file. Findings are deduped by resolved path so a project root does not double-count its venv, and each root is indexed separately so cross-module NewType resolution stays within a project.

## What is left

The all-rules sweep. It was deferred onto mlp-kzi, which has now landed: enabling every rule brought ML108/ML109 into play, and their import resolution scanned the whole module index, so a sweep was quadratic in the size of each root and an all-rules run was killed at 52 minutes unfinished. CONTRIBUTING_RULES.md still carries a warning saying so and telling authors to name one rule at a time.

Run the all-rules sweep now that resolution is a bucket lookup, then replace that warning with what the sweep actually costs. If it is now routine, the warning goes entirely.
close_reason:
The recipes landed in 7f2edbe: just corpus-lint and just corpus-diff over scripts/corpus_lint.py, with the corpus location in a gitignored .corpus.toml and a walkthrough in CONTRIBUTING_RULES.md. What was outstanding was the all-rules sweep, deferred onto mlp-kzi, and the warning in the docs saying it was impractical.

mlp-kzi has landed, so the sweep was run: 60,537 files across 11 roots, 313 unparseable skipped, 400s for all 21 rules against 166s for one. Per-file cost no longer tracks root size — 3.74ms at 645 files and 3.72ms at 12,993, where before the fix the same two roots cost 7.22ms and 160.43ms. The warning is replaced in e6212d6 with the measured cost, and _build_index's docstring no longer describes the resolution mechanism mlp-kzi replaced.

The sweep's own finding is filed as mlp-1kx: ML500 is 188,854 of the 215,000-odd hits, 88% of the report, partly from short spellings that are ordinary identifiers ('ax' flagged as 'axe' on every matplotlib axes variable) and partly from correct hits on third-party code nobody will rewrite. Whoever reads an all-rules report next will hit that before anything else.

title: ML701's string-constant table has no scope model
description:
mlp-91c gave ML701 a module-level table of names bound to string literals, so that `ZoneInfo(_DEFAULT_ZONE_NAME)` over `_DEFAULT_ZONE_NAME = "UTC"` is recognised as the invented `ZoneInfo("UTC")` it is. The table records a name the first time it sees a string literal assigned to it and never revises that, so it is wrong in both directions.

## Too permissive: a rebound name still reads as constant

Both of these fire, and neither should. The zone is derived from a runtime value, which is exactly the false positive mlp-91c was filed to remove.

    import zoneinfo

    _TZ = "UTC"

    def resolve(request, d):
        _TZ = request.tz_name              # shadows the module constant
        fallback = zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(_TZ)
        return d.tzinfo or fallback        # ML701 fires

    import zoneinfo

    _TZ = "UTC"
    _TZ = discover()                       # no longer a constant

    def resolve(d):
        fallback = zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(_TZ)
        return d.tzinfo or fallback        # ML701 fires

## Too narrow: a local string constant is not resolved

Silent, though the zone is as invented as the module-level spelling. Documented in the rule's exemptions as a known limit rather than left implicit.

    import zoneinfo

    def resolve(d):
        name = "UTC"
        fallback = zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(name)
        return d.tzinfo or fallback        # silent

## Why it was left this way

Deliberate, not overlooked. Local strings are rebound far more often than module-level ones, and mistaking a rebound local for a constant yields a false positive — the expensive direction, and the very class of bug mlp-91c fixed. Module-level-only was the conservative line. The rebinding cases above show the conservative line is not actually safe, so the real fix is a scope model rather than a wider table.

## Where it is

src/ml_lints/rules/ml701_timezone_substitution.py — `ML701._note_string_constant`, `self._module_constant_names`, consumed by `_is_a_constant_zone_identity`.

## Note

Same defect family as mlp-2o7 (a class-body zone binding leaking into module scope): ML701 keeps ad-hoc name tables instead of modelling Python scope. Two tables now have the problem, so a shared scope model would settle both. Worth doing together.

title: ML701's message does not say what a named fallback is bound to
description:
ML701 renders the fallback expression into its message by unparsing the node it matched.
When the fallback is a name, that yields the name and nothing else, so the message
asserts a substitution without showing the zone being substituted:

```
psycopg/_tz.py:45:9: ML701 Timezone silently substituted with 'zi'; take the zone from
                     the caller that has it, or raise if nobody does
```

`zi` is bound to `timezone.utc` sixteen lines earlier. The reader has to go and find
that to see why this is a finding at all -- and the binding may be anywhere in the
scope, or at module level.

Compare the literal case, which needs no lookup:

```
api/db/user_ops.py:360:9: ML701 Timezone silently substituted with
                          'zoneinfo.ZoneInfo('UTC')'; ...
```

The issue's own "what already works" section credits exactly this property of the ML700
and ML701 messages -- naming the offending value and the consequence in one line, with
no need to run `--explain`. The named-fallback shape added in 8fa027f is the one place
that no longer holds.

## Where it is

`src/ml_lints/rules/ml701_timezone_substitution.py`. `_report_substitution` takes an
already-rendered string; callers pass `ast.unparse(node)`. The binding that made the
name a zone is recorded in `_module_zone_names` / `_FunctionFrame.zone_names`, both of
which are `set[str]` and keep only the name.

## Fix

Carry the rendered binding alongside the name (a `dict[str, str]`, or a small frozen
dataclass if the sets grow other fields) and render as `zi (timezone.utc)`. Note a name
may be bound more than once -- `zi` is assigned both `ZoneInfo(sname)` and
`timezone.utc` -- so decide which binding to show, or show the first zone-valued one.
acceptance_criteria: A finding whose fallback is a name shows the zone that name is bound to, so the message is actionable without reading the rest of the scope.

title: ML701 leaks a class-body zone binding into module scope
description:
ML701's zone-name tracking keeps module-level bindings in one file-wide set and
function-local bindings on the function frame, so a local goes out of scope with its
function (fixed in 8fa027f). A binding in a *class body* belongs to neither, and falls
through to the module set -- where it stays visible to every function in the file.

```python
import zoneinfo


class Config:
    FALLBACK = zoneinfo.ZoneInfo("UTC")


def label_for(name: str, FALLBACK: str) -> str:
    return name or FALLBACK          # ML701 fires; FALLBACK here is a plain str
```

Verified against the shipped rule.

This is the same defect class as the cross-function leak already fixed, and it
contradicts the rule's own documented exemption, which promises a name is recognised
"only when it is bound in the same file, either at module level or earlier in the same
scope".

## Where it is

`src/ml_lints/rules/ml701_timezone_substitution.py`, `ML701._note_zone_binding` --
`self._function_stack[-1].zone_names if self._function_stack else self._module_zone_names`.
A class body is not a function, so it takes the module branch.

## Severity

Low in practice. A class attribute is normally read as `self.FALLBACK` or
`Config.FALLBACK`, which is an `ast.Attribute` and never matches the bare-`ast.Name`
lookup -- so the leak only bites when an unrelated *bare local* elsewhere in the file
shares the attribute's name. Worth fixing for consistency with the documented
behaviour rather than for the findings it removes.

## Fix

Push a scope for `ClassDef` the way `FunctionDef` does, and have `_is_zone_name`
consult it. Note the Python semantics differ from a function scope: a class body's
names are visible to the statements in that body but not to methods defined inside it,
so a class scope should not be consulted from within a nested function.
acceptance_criteria: A zone bound in a class body is not treated as a zone by unrelated bare names elsewhere in the file; the documented 'same scope' exemption holds for class bodies as it now does for functions.

title: ML703: calendar arithmetic must live in a blessed date module
description:
Deferred from the ML700-ML702 epic (mlp-u1f). The aspiration rule: day-or-larger calendar arithmetic outside one designated module is a violation, because that module is the only place a real ZoneInfo is guaranteed to have been applied.

This is the only rule in the class that would make the defect extinct rather than netting it -- it is a positive architectural statement rather than a blacklist, and it is self-reinforcing.

Two costs blocked it, and the second is the binding one.

1. Allowlist length. Measured against ../casey_ai: at day-or-larger scale there are 24 non-test timedelta(days=) sites outside api/date_utils.py, which is an unusable allowlist. Restricted to weeks= there are 4 -- api/calendar_sync.py:143 and :144, api/routes/schedule/core.py:226, api/maps_client.py:468 -- which is short enough to be real. Start there if this is revived.

2. It is not expressible as an ml-lints rule today. 'Outside api/date_utils.py' is a consumer-specific fact. cli.py parses only select, extend_select, ignore, exclude and respect_gitignore -- there is no per-rule configuration mechanism at all. This rule needs one built first, and would be inert in every repo that has not configured it.

Prerequisite: per-rule configuration in cli.py. Do not start this before that exists.

title: TypeScript counterparts for ML700-ML702
description:
ML700, ML701 and ML702 are Python-only. When the TypeScript port's conformance gates land (mlp-v00.10 metadata, mlp-v00.12 behavioural corpus), all three will need TS counterparts or an explicit per-rule exclusion.

Nothing is broken today -- the gates do not exist yet, so Python-only rules pass. This is a note so the three do not go missing when the gates are switched on.

Consider whether the whole TIME_CORRECTNESS category is worth porting at all. The rules encode a hazard specific to Python's datetime/ZoneInfo split; the equivalent JS hazard (Temporal vs Date) has a different shape and may deserve different rules rather than transliterations.
